utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While the witness is on his way, Mr. Sepenuk, are you able to tell me any more about the translation of the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, I think Mr. Visnjic can perhaps enlighten you a bit more on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've had consultations with the translation section, and the answer that they have given is quite definite. They said it will take several months. I can explain further. It's a collection of documents, combat reports from the Supreme Command Staff. There are some 70 reports, each of which has between 10 and 12 pages. We filed those reports for the first time in June, but then we withdrew them due to other priorities because we had witnesses coming in the meantime with other documents. And in one of our most recent requests, we submitted those documents for translation. In the meantime, we did withdraw some documents because we felt it would be too difficult or too complicated for the translation section. One of them is the war diary that Mr. Hannis has examined the previous witness about for the simple reason that the document is in handwriting and is very lengthy, but from previous statements by the witness we learned that this war diary is a kind of summary of the combat reports which we have already handed in for translation, so that all I can say is that our intention was to hand in all the combat reports of the 3rd Army which we consider to be important to get a complete picture, but we thought that Mr. Ackerman would do so as part of his documents, so we also withdrew those from the translation section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying they are not part of the 70 reports then?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. So I'm referring exclusively to documents that we received from the National Council under the heading of combat reports of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, do you have anything to say on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I cannot see how we could file any response accepting or consenting to the admission of these documents without being able to read the translated versions. I agree with Mr. Ackerman in what he said yesterday. It's next to impossible to have anything useful to say about documents which are in Cyrillic many times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but the question I think's a rather different one. Does it mean that the Ojdanic case has to proceed without them or -- would that be your position or do we go home for six months while the translators work on the translations or what --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's a practical solution we're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I do not believe that the documents ought to or can be received into evidence, perhaps marked for identity, but I cannot see how documents not in a language of the Tribunal could be received into evidence. I understand from what Mr. Visnjic said is that it is probable and possible that they have some relevance in the case of Mr. Ackerman, and perhaps that might provide a solution in respect to some of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What it would appear Mr. Ackerman has done, and obviously he can speak for himself if he disagrees, but he has very carefully selected what he sees as really relevant to his case and has prepared, it would appear, a very focused case. We have yet to hear that of course, I'm maybe giving him too much credit. It may not be his intention to amplify along these lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think, though, that perhaps -- and we will file within a time-frame earlier than the 14-days response time, we'll file a formal response to the application of the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't need to do that because the Chamber will not consider these documents as they are and will not consider the application in relation to the ones that are not translated in its current form. Before we could even begin to look at this issue properly it would be necessary for Mr. Visnjic to I think formulate a quite different motion with extracts from these documents explaining their relevance and asking us for indulgence in allowing him time to get this done and present them, and let us see if, in fact, he can even begin to make a case for resources being expended in this way and perhaps indulgence being granted to him. Now, Mr. Visnjic, I think that's the very least that we can expect of you at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm talking now about this collection of reports of the Supreme Command Staff that we have considered as a possibility to provide only the extracts referring to the 3rd Army or to certain joint factors relating to NATO activities in the territory and so on. In those reports there are certainly parts which perhaps need not be part of this case, but you know when we work with a part of a document, an extract, the Prosecution objects and asks for the whole document. So in my view, if we look at the relevance of those documents, they have two-fold, a part of them as specific relating to the 3rd Army and what was going on there and others relate to the overall activities that General Ojdanic engaged in while he was working in the command of the supreme staff. So there's always two ways of looking at it. There -- I could focus on parts which might be more relevant than the rest, which I also consider them to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, how many documents are in this -- in this motion are already translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From that collection, two have been used as an example, and I think they have already been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does the motion, though, relate to any other documents apart from the supreme-- apart from the minutes -- apart from the combat reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there's only one other document - I'm afraid I don't have all the documents on me - and that is the rules on the responsibilities of the Supreme Command Staff, which is quite a lengthy document. It has been rejected by the translation section because special instructions are required from the Chamber because the document is about 30 pages long. And this document is relevant because it clearly shows the function of each of the witnesses that have appeared in this case, including General Ojdanic himself while he was deputy Chief of Staff and later also during the operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you can take it, Mr. Stamp, you've made sufficient submissions for the present to enable us to deal with this particular motion, and we will make a decision about the motion as it stands. That may be an interim decision, though, in this process, but it will enable us to consider exactly of what we should require of Mr. Visnjic before proceeding further. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe it's not wise to continue this discussion any further, Your Honour, but I do have a thought or two that I would like to put on the record. I think what we're seeing today is pretty much the tip of a rather large iceberg. I think the translation problems for numbers 5 and 6 in this group are huge compared to what some of the rest of us are looking at. And when you start looking at what this means in terms of this trial, you must begin to focus on concepts of justice, I believe. If you consider this case was being tried in Serbia before a group of Serbian judges, this problem wouldn't arise because every document that Defence counsel thought was relevant to their case would be, if seen by the judges as relevant, brought to their attention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would arise, though, in relation to the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Not necessarily, the Prosecution could also be Serbian, Your Honour, so there would be no need to translate any documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witnesses haven't tended to be Serbian, Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There could have been some of that, but nothing compared to what we have here. Because we have decided to proceed with these cases in this somewhat artificial forum where the languages are English and French, the official languages, then we must proceed with documents that are translated into those languages. For no other reason, if there's no other reason, it is because it is extremely important for Your Honours to be able to see what those say, and I think it's not -- you know, I know that Judge Kamenova can read Serbo-Croatian pretty well, but I don't think that's sufficient for your entire Chamber. And it may very well be that there is one part of this Tribunal that simply can't measure up to the speed at which we are trying to move these cases through here, and that's the translation section. I've spoken to people about it, very high level in this Tribunal, and they believe they have working for them about everybody that's available, that's capable to do this kind of work in the whole world that's available to be here. And there's not much more to be done about it and if it requires we have to slow down a bit, we have to slow down a bit as much as I hate to say that. I'm tired of being in this case. I'm ready to go home, but the bottom line when somebody looks back at us 20 or 30 years from now we want to have them say we did our best to do justice here, and I don't think we can do that if we're dealing with a bunch of documents that none of us can read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree with all you said, Mr. Ackerman, but we also don't want history to look back and say what a mess they made of that by allowing all that unnecessary drivel to hold up the proceedings. So we have to look carefully at what it is that needs to be translated. Maybe I did you too much credit, I don't know, but I got the impression that's exactly what you've done in preparing your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's exactly what I've done and I would hope my colleague have done the same. This case is a dynamic thing that goes on here and one day that seems really important that you get documents and send the translation all of a sudden a month later is not important anymore. So what we've done is withdrawn documents from translation when we've realised those documents were no longer relevant for one reason or another. And we've sent a great deal more documents for translation than we have asked to be translated finally in the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For me, maybe it's different for my colleagues, I'm speaking for myself, but for me it's not good enough to say we want to give you the whole story, we want to give you the whole history of the combat reports, that's not how adversarial proceedings work. Therefore, we have to look more closely at what Mr. Visnjic's real requirements are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're using the combat reports that we think are relevant. We haven't translated the others. That's how we're proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There may be a misunderstanding here about what the process is meant to do and from the Defence point of view there is an obligation, just as there is on the Prosecution, to focus on issues that are relevant to the case, not to say: Have a bunch of documents and go make what you will of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I was suggesting is focus does not stay the same all the time. For instance, many of us translated documents that we were going to use in the cross-examination of General Clark, and all of a sudden General Clark wasn't there. We couldn't wait until the last minute and say we can't bring him, Your Honour, because we haven't translated the documents we need to cross-examine him with. So there's some unnecessary translation that has happened there. That's happened in more than one case. We're down to a point now where I think all of us can pretty much do a pretty good job of winnowing and getting where we need to go, and I think everybody will commit to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me make it also clear that we have encouraged the use of paper or written product because of the limitations there are on live court time, so we in a sense may have contributed to the situation. Although I'm not in a position to compare this case with any others. I don't know whether we are in any different position of whether other cases just have the same situation volume of material. However, these are things on which we will ponder and a decision will be issued and that will hopefully give guidance on how to proceed with this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may have misinformed you, I didn't quite understand. Your question was how many documents from our motion of the 16th of October have been translated. I can tell you that about half of those documents have been translated, but most of the untranslated documents are the collection of combat reports that I have referred to. The other documents have been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was my understanding, Mr. Visnjic, and I just wanted the figure for that. Now, Mr. Stamp, how long will it take you to deal with the ones which have been translated? Was that the issue on which you said you would require until Friday or was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was a separate motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Separate motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I believe in respect to the translated documents that we received we could respond by Monday at the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we will order you to respond by Monday so that we can deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Radinovic, sorry to have held up your evidence, but this is a fairly important issue and had to be addressed this morning. Your cross-examination by Mr. Stamp for the Prosecution will commence in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth continues to apply to your evidence, and before we proceed with that cross-examination can you tell me whether your researches bore any fruit yesterday in respect of the matter left outstanding with Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This is a document, a notification for the public by Radio Television Serbia about the meeting held on the 4th of May, 1999, with the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, attended by the commander of the 3rd Army and the head of the MUP staff in Kosovo and Metohija and other officials, that is what stated in the announcement without an indication of their names. At that meeting, as stated in the announcement Milan Lukic and General Pavkovic briefed about the situation in Kosovo and Metohija and made an assessment of the success of the defence against the NATO aggression against the Siptar forces. If I may consult paper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me say, it was Mr. Ackerman's question that was outstanding and not Mr. Ivetic. And I think you may have answered it, unless Mr. Ackerman wishes -- no, he's indicating he doesn't require any further information, so thank you for that. Now, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the number of the document in the e-court, K01239962.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did you manage to get that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was in my notes. I noted it down. I simply hadn't brought the document with me, as I failed to bring some others with me as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. The document was properly disclosed by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, General Radinovic. Before I proceed --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- In respect of what you just said about Radio Television Serbia notification to the public about this meeting on the 4th of May, did that notification indicate whether or not General Ojdanic was at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I just mentioned that. I don't know whether it is -- has entered the record, but I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, it was not on the transcript, and I didn't hear it. Let's move on. You have testified at this Tribunal before in the case certainly against Stanislav Galic and the case against General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that it is appropriate for an expert in dealing with his conclusions to cite the sources that he draws upon in which to arrive at those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And more so if the matter is a controversial matter or an important matter?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what you mean. I don't understand the question, if it's a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to start by asking you some of the sources you used. Let's focus firstly on what you had to say about General Ojdanic's biography. You said that he at some point abandoned his Ph.D. Because his dissertation wasn't approved, but you didn't provide the source. Did someone tell you that or did you find that in some document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This can be found in the documents of the teaching council of the military academy because it is the obligation of the council, when considering applications for a dissertation, to collect views of the General Staff as to the significance of the topic of the dissertation for the development of the army in a particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You said that this was an important matter for us to understand the role of General Ojdanic, but you did not cite that source in your report. Is there a reason why you did not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's absolutely no reason. It is information that can easily be obtained, and I felt that in this report there are so many more significant sources mentioned. So I noted this down simply as one of the elements contributing to the personal and professional biography of General Ojdanic. If necessary, I can provide that document from a meeting of the teaching council of the military academy without any difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We don't have time for that. I'm just concerned now about the reasons, if any, why you didn't cite them. At paragraph 13, page 61, of your report you made the claim that General Ojdanic and General Perisic didn't get along, relations was very cold. And you base that on a statement that General Perisic didn't attend General Ojdanic's appointment when he was appointed to be head of the 3rd Army -- sorry, the Uzice Corps. Is that all the sources you have for that assertion that there was some sort of coldness or a lack of an amicable relationship between General Ojdanic and General Perisic or were there other sources that you did not cite in your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to certain facts, not just sources. This refers to the commander of the 1st Army, not the Uzice Corps, not that it's very important, just for the sake of precision. General Perisic was not there, although he was duty-bound to be present at the handover of duties, and he did not provide any justification for his absence. Secondly, General Perisic was head of the General Staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I'm asking is this, you said General Perisic was not there and was duty-bound to be there, and you draw the conclusion that that indicates that there was some sort of lack of an amicable relationship. What's the source of that information and why didn't you put it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't on the basis of that fact that he was not present at the handover of duties that I drew the conclusion that their relations were not very good. There were other reasons and I'll tell you what they are. Just bear with me --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a minute, but that is not exactly what I am asking you about. You cited that as a reason why you made that statement. Now you're telling us that that was not the only reason and there are other reasons. The direction of my question is: Why is it that the other reasons on which you based your opinion are not put in our report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are in my report. It says that the General Staff, which was headed by General Perisic, did not give approval for General Ojdanic's research and chosen topic on advancing the monitoring of combat-readiness. There's no General Staff in the world that would not support such a topic, but General Perisic did not. There can be no other reason but some sort of personal reason or other nonprofessional reason, non-scholarly reason. This topic was a very important one, it was very necessary to research that topic, and it has not been researched to date; unfortunately, the system has remained the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, General, kindly forgive me for interrupting. Did you see that dissertation yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was one of the members of the commission for evaluating the appropriateness and significance of the topic. The dissertation was not complete, it was in the initial stages of submission for approval. There was General Cubura, unfortunately he is deceased, and somebody else, I can't remember who. And we were members of the commission. We wrote a positive report since it was a very significant topic, very well developed, containing everything that such a topic implies, and we were extremely surprised that it was not accepted. Based on this and based on other facts and also based on the facts I established in analysing the relationship of General Ojdanic and General Perisic at the collegium meetings and their behaviour in their professional relations, General Perisic, when dealing with General Ojdanic as a deputy Chief of the General Staff, according to the rules and so on, I drew the conclusion from all this that their relations were not good and that this could affect the functioning of the command and control system.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which year was the dissertation or uncompleted dissertation submitted?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just an application with an overview of the contents, the aim, the procedure, so it's just an application for the commission to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be absolutely certain, but I think it was in 1994, 1995, maybe 1996, I'm not sure, but this can be established. I just can't recall it at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the time, where was General Ojdanic posted?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure whether he was already the commander of the 1st Army or the Chief of Staff of the 1st Army, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You further go on to say that General Ojdanic had no influence on the situation in Kosovo when he was deputy Chief of the General Staff and he never received information from units about the situation in Kosovo when he was deputy Chief of Staff. That's at paragraph 18, page 196 -- sorry, paragraph 18, page 65 to 66 of your report. And you cite footnotes -- in footnote 130 a document that we have not been given. I just say that for the record. But in footnote 131 you cite another document in support of this assertion, and that's Exhibit 923 -- P923. Could we bring --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Stamp, that the collegium session minutes of the 10th of August, 1998, are not available?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Exhibit -- footnote 130, may I just get the date correct, it's the -- it was corrected to the 7th of August, 1997, in the addendum 5, but they were not available, they were not supplied to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought all the collegium minutes were available. That's wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I only wish to confirm this. I received the collegium meetings as a collection from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Our checks indicate that we did not have that one for the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you still don't have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And we still don't have it, but I will reconfirm and get back to footnote 130 after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The one we have, General, is footnote 131, P923, and I would like us just to have a look at that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, but it's K0520537 for the collegium of the 7th of August, 1998. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: P923, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You cited that one to support the claim that General Ojdanic is saying that he's not receiving daily operation reports from the units in the field. Can we first look at page 15 of that document, it is page 16 in the B/C/S version. In the -- at the top of the B/C/S page you see General Ojdanic speaking. Can you just read what he says there? I just want to check the translation.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginning of the page, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I demand that as your deputy I receive the combat report of the commander of the 3rd Army, and I propose that that same report be received by the assistant for the ground forces and the chief of the first administration. Now I would like to make a suggestion and a proposal, General, sir."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you see General Perisic responding to that as the next speaker, and he sees -- and he says to General Martinovic to deal with it but make sure that the deputy receives it in addition to the others. Now, isn't General Galic -- sorry, General Perisic and General Ojdanic speaking about one particular report? Do you recall that from reading this collegium minute?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to see the whole record. I can't make that conclusion just based on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would like to take you through it because I think this is important. If we look at page 7 of the document - and this is the B/C/S page 6 - do we have it there -- sorry, the B/C/S page 8. I'm going to the bottom of the English version, which is the top of the -- of page 8 of the English version. General Panic, Miodrag Panic, makes a report. Who is Miodrag Panic, by the way, or who was he at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Panic, I think that at that time he was the assistant for the ground force, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So he was making a report in respect to the ground forces, and he says: "There are no major changes regarding the KoV. This group has been moved a little from the 549, but that is all there is in that area and within the jurisdiction of the corps commander. In accordance with your order and review of your order, the 3rd Army commander has sent a draft decision by telegram for approval." And he goes on to deal what the proposal is of the draft decision that was sent by the 3rd Army commander. If we look at that proposal and turn to page 8 of the English version but remain on that page -- B/C/S page 8, you see that General Panic in respect to this document proposes that after this collegium General Martinovic, General Bojovic, and General Dimitrijevic, and I propose to you whether or not to accept this proposal of the 3rd Army or not. Move to page 9 of the English version -- sorry, page 10 of the English version, and that's at the top of page 10 of the English version. And this is the bottom of page 10 of the B/C/S version. In discussing this document General Martinovic says: "I propose that you accept the decision or the draft decision of the 3rd Army commander regarding the provision of security for the road from Pristina across the Dulje pass..." And further on on page 10 of the English document, which is page 11 of the B/C/S, if you just look at page 11 of the B/C/S, we see that General Perisic and General Bojovic are discussing this draft telegram that the 3rd Army commander sent with his proposals on the road, and they are dealing with it as it -- as if it's a matter of some importance because it must be resolved in agreement with the MUP. And the last part of it I want to show you, and that is a discussion in respect to this document, is page 14 of the English version, the middle of that page, which is page 15 of the B/C/S, you see that General Perisic says or orders: "With Ojdanic and Bojovic and also others who must analyse the draft decision of the 3rd Army commander and propose what is to be done in terms of improving security on the road Pristina-Stimlje-Suva Reka- Prizren-Djakovica and Urosevac, and again this way." I would just like you to have a look at that. General Perisic is appointing Ojdanic and Bojovic to deal with it. And we come back to page 15, which is the first bit I read to you, in which General Ojdanic says: "As your deputy, I request" -- well, you say -- I think the translation was that: "I demand that I receive the 3rd Army commander's report ..." And General Perisic says: "First of all, the report you deal with it and make sure the deputy receives it ..." Why I took you through this is, firstly, you cite this as to say or in support of a statement that Ojdanic, General Ojdanic is saying he's not receiving the daily operation reports. What General Ojdanic is saying, clearly from the context of this collegium, is that he did not receive one telegram, a report or a proposal sent by the 3rd Army commander, the day before. Isn't that plain from a reading of this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidently not. It's not evident, that is, if you look at the nuances in General Ojdanic's request he says: "As your deputy, I request that I receive," and the verb form in the original is "dobijam" it's continuous form, not one-time form. There is a distinction in the Serbian language between "dobijam" and "dobijem" so he is saying that he is not receiving the reports, and he is requesting from the Chief of the General Staff that he also receive these reports on an ongoing basis. That was the reason for my conclusion, that he was not receiving the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you, there must be a noun there for "report" or "reports." Is it singular or plural? It's been translated into the English as "reports," but what is the actual word? Could you just tell me the word for -- that's in that minute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the page be brought back, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is page 15 in the English, the top of page 16 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army sends a combat report, one combat report every day. In this sentence in which General Ojdanic is requesting that the reports be sent to him, the -- the verb he uses is "dobijam" which means on a regular or ongoing basis, but the noun is in the singular. The noun is in the singular, but the verb is in the continuous form. That can be a contradiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that -- now, do you have in your bag with you -- well, in fact, we can see it on the -- well, it would be easier if you referred to the hard copy of your own report in B/C/S. Do you have that available? And just look at that footnote in the B/C/S version of your own report and tell me if you've quoted it word for word for if you've altered any of the words from the collegium report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you be so kind as to tell me what footnote it is, the footnote number?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Footnote 131.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question's simple: Have you used the singular or the plural in your own report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my report I used the singular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And first may I just ask you to read it, just translate it to me, that you said the singular report, and that's at page 17, line 2. The translation I have here is not only that it is singular, is that you said that: "I request to receive this report." You are speaking about a particular report -- sorry, General Ojdanic here is speaking about a particular report. So have a look at it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you have a problem here, Mr. Stamp, because CLSS have translated it in the way that the witness has invited us to understand it, that the verb is an ongoing -- is an indication of an ongoing practice, and it's perfectly consistent with that for CLSS to have translated reports in the plural into English. Now, that -- you've got his evidence, you're now asking the same question again. I think you should move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The next aspect of this document I'd like to ask you about, General, is this. I have it, and I represent to you that this is what happened, the deputy chief for the ground forces says that there was a post that was sent by telegram by the command of the 3rd Army. He recommends that a group, including General Dimitrijevic himself and himself consider it and propose it to accept it. General Perisic in the discussion indicates that it is a very important proposal and rejects his recommendation and instead appoints his deputy, General Ojdanic, to review it. General Ojdanic asks to receive it and General Perisic says, Yes, he's to get it. Does that indicate to you that General Ojdanic is out of the loop or does not -- is treated as somebody without any responsibility in the collegium?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether he was respected in the collegium. I can only answer the question as to whether he received the combat reports he should have received. According to my understanding of what he said here, I understood that he was not receiving them and was requesting that they be sent to him. He should have received them because it was his duty to prepare briefings for the Chief of the General Staff. So it was his operational task, and how could he carry it out unless he received reports from the subordinate commands? That's how I understood the gist of General Ojdanic's request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Radinovic, there are two different concepts here, they may be the same thing but -- and it may be my misunderstanding, but the footnote is dealing with combat reports or a combat report. The proposal that's being discussed at the collegium, would that be contained in the combat report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the proposal of the commander of the 3rd Army on the engagement of forces -- yes, that would have been in the report. So what the commander proposes he includes in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On some occasions, it's a separate document, a proposal, but it would certainly have been included in the combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But we see here that in this case what they are discussing is a draft decision that was sent by telegram the day before, I've showed you that. But let me ask you about combat reports, the operational reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you are saying they are two separate documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is clear from -- it is my submission when reading the minutes that they are speaking about -- and if we look at page 7 of the English, paragraph -- page 8 of the B/C/S, a draft decision by telegram for approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, how does any of that -- if they are two separate documents, how does the fact that the -- that that is a separate document -- how does that assist in interpreting the reference to report?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness uses that to support an assertion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I understand what he uses it -- but I don't understand why you went through the whole of the minute which is about another document to tell us how to interpret a reference to the combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There are two issues. One is that the paragraph in which they -- the witness cites this document, the paragraph which purports to show that General Ojdanic was not within the loop of management of the General Staff, he was not given significant responsibility, and he was not aware of what was going on. When - and I will invite the Court later on - when one goes through the relevant part of this collegium report, those parts that I cited, one will see how the discussion developed to the point where General Ojdanic says, Give me a copy of the report. And it does not indicate that he was somebody who was not given responsibility, quite the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, these are submissions later. I'm just trying to understand why -- how the reference to the telegram containing the draft --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Was relevant to working out the meaning of this particular quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If they had been in the same document, I would have understood the point. I'm now slightly baffled by the approach you've taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The members of the collegium are discussing one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document is referred -- the document is a telegram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, and Ojdanic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And Ojdanic refers to it as a report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He doesn't have the report, the combat report, and he maybe never got any combat reports. How can we conclude from reading this whether he got combat reports on a regular basis or not? He didn't have this one, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I do not represent to the witness or to the Court that this says that he was receiving combat reports on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I understand that, Mr. Stamp, but anyway you continue the way you want to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Stamp, I would just like that we have to discern between two, first is this telegraphic draft from the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And the regular reports from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: -- The regular combat reports. Now, as we go through it we have to see that these two issues do not mix up because there is one separate thing, that is, the third telegraphic draft from the 3rd Army, and then this -- where Ojdanic was asked to review and all, and then there are the regular reports when he is complaining. So I think if you keep this in mind, that will clarify things instead of baffling.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: At least myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on from that. The exhibit is P923 and I'd just invite the Court to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Combat reports, regular combat reports by the armies are normally sent to the operations section of the General Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were sent to the General Staff, and they were received by the operations sector. That was the part of the General Staff in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the operations sector would compile from all those combat reports that it received from the various armies a report which it circulates among the members of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In which case General Ojdanic would be receiving the reports of the operations centre which refers to reports from the various armies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The General Staff does not function like that in the peacetime. A report from the supreme commander doesn't go to the Presidency in peacetime, it goes like that in wartime. So there was no written report of the General Staff, it's just that operations report from army commands were received and at collegium meetings there would be briefings if there was something important to consider. From what I understood from this collegium meeting, General Ojdanic wasn't receiving those reports and that's why he requested them, so that he could have an informed opinion and take part in the discussion. He wanted first-hand information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wouldn't the combat reports or the daily operations reports that were sent by the armies be registered in the archives of the operations sector of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you saying --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- They would --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- They would but he would not have access to those archives?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have had access to the archives, but why would he go every day to the operations sector and ask them for them? He should have received them ex officio, that's why he asked the Chief of the General Staff that he receive the combat reports of the army. He was just wondering and he was even protesting in a way over the fact that he wasn't receiving them. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The other thing you say is that as the person who had to brief the Chief of General Staff, they were necessary for his work to be done. Are you saying that General Ojdanic remained as deputy Chief of General Staff until the 22nd of June, 1998, and was so derelict in his duties that he remained there without receiving combat reports from the armies and the strategic groups?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know really what you're asking me. I analysed the documents that were available to me, not relationships within the General Staff or the conduct of its individual members. In my report, in this section, I speak of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, General, General, you do make many statements about the relationships in the General Staff and the conduct of individual members, you do in your report. All I'm asking you is this: In your opinion as an expert, wouldn't General Ojdanic be extremely derelict in his duty to remain as deputy Chief of General Staff for a period of time without getting operation reports from the armies and other strategic groups? That's within your expertise to comment upon.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from this document I concluded that he was a deputy Chief of the General Staff who did not receive these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's a factual conclusion that you're making that he did not receive it. I represent to you that this document does not indicate that he was not receiving them. What I'm asking you for now is your opinion as an expert a deputy Chief of General Staff who does not receive the regular operation reports from the strategic groups would be extremely derelict in his duties; isn't that your view?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've -- Mr. Radinovic, we've had repeated evidence in this case of how meticulous a man General Ojdanic was, and Mr. Stamp is saying to you a man like that surely wouldn't let this happen and not do anything about it. It would show a dereliction of duty. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Presiding Judge, this paragraph that I've read from the collegium meeting where he says: "I demand to receive combat reports ..." Speaks precisely to that. No deputy Chief of General Staff likes to hear a demand worded in this way. He put it very strongly, so he wanted these reports in order to be able to do his job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How frequently were these reports submitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reports are sent every day, interim reports were sent as necessary, as required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And by this time, General Ojdanic had been in the post for about seven weeks?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Or may I just remind you, you said, and it is evident before the Court, that General Ojdanic was appointed deputy Chief of the General Staff in 1996, in July 1996 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, it's my mistake, there's a reference --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- Two years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the reference to June 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: June 1998 is the date when he's requesting -- when the witness purports that he's requesting to receive daily operation reports, 22nd of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, sorry, it is my mistake, it's a period of two years. So is it not rather odd that he would let that period of time elapse without receiving these or doing something about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not saying that he hadn't received a single report, but I do assert that he requested them. So it's probably the case that he didn't receive them regularly. It is a fact that struck me as a person who dealt with this problem, and that seems to indicate that as the deputy General Ojdanic was not regularly informed of what he should have been regularly informed. So he's saying that: I demand that I be informed regularly, too, as deputy chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Did you check of any -- did you check about any orders coming from his boss with whom he had fallen out, stating that he should not be shown those reports? Did you come across any such order or any such indication that these reports should find their way up, leaving him behind, I mean taking a digression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And then why didn't he put his house in order so that this chain of command or the channel to which these reports go up is observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not a question for me; it's probably a question for General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, that is a question for you. You are an expert.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that that's not the natural course of things. It would be normal that everyone in the chain of command would be authorised to receive reports and to receive them. That's why I pointed this fact out. This fact indicates that something was wrong. If the deputy wasn't receiving reports regularly, that was something I could not miss, I could not fail to mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, I suggest to you that in the extract I just showed you from the collegium minutes of the 22nd of June, when General Ojdanic requested to receive the report, singular, he was speaking of the special telegram that had been sent to him, that had been sent to the chief of the ground forces, not the daily operation reports, as you represent. Do you --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the meaning it has in Serbian, I'm telling you he was requesting to receive reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Have you ever met General Ojdanic before 1999? Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you say you have known him very well?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not too well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have you spoken to him in preparation of this report or while you were preparing this report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We talked about many things, but not this report because I thought that the report was my work, my obligation, and he had no obligation with regard to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I take it that while you were preparing the report you had conversations with him but you refrained from speaking about the report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we never discussed my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We met at the office of Mr. Visnjic. I wanted to see him when he was released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the office of the Defence team in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the point of you meeting Mr. Ojdanic other than to discuss matters relating to the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is a prominent general -- rather, he was a prominent general, he had been in detention, and I wanted to see him just to say hello.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a man that you don't know very well? I find that very difficult to understand, bearing in mind the role that you were asked to play in this case. Do you wish to comment further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I believed, in view of the role I'm playing in his defence, that it is only a matter of courtesy to see him, to say hello, so ask after his health, to initiate that sort of contact as a human being, to express concern and care because I simply had that role. But I thought it made no sense to talk about my work because it was my obligation and I had to rely on the documentation available to me to produce a proper piece of work and I didn't need his assistance for that. If I had needed his assistance, I would have requested an interview, but I thought it was not necessary. I thought it was a matter of good manners to come and see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we to conclude, therefore, that you have a measure of personal sympathy for Mr. Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I fail to understand your reason then for wanting to see him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you to appreciate and understand that, if you are able to. I did have a role in his defence and I had a duty to make a report on his command competence, but I thought it was a matter of elementary good manners to come and see him, say hello, ask after his health, and extend some kind of moral support by doing so, but no more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me also make it clear that I could have understood circumstances in which it would be appropriate for you to meet him to discuss the case, but you say that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That didn't happen for the simple reason that I wanted to produce a report that would reflect my opinion without any outside influence, because outside influence would only disrupt my line of thinking and I did not want any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to follow-up on that, how many times did you meet him at Mr. Visnjic's office, once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who invited you there? I mean, how was the meeting arranged?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked counsel Visnjic to enable me to see General Ojdanic. It was my initiative because I thought -- I thought I should.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I got into this because I thought from reading your report that you had spoken to him about it. But, you know, what I think doesn't really matter. Can I ask you about one or two things that you have said. You said at paragraph 159, page 119 of your report, that the Chief of the General Staff decided to wait ten days -- now, I don't want to have to go through the whole thing because time is limited, but in the context of the whole thing, about what you have discussed here, how is it you became aware that the Chief of the General Staff decided to wait for at least ten days? Because when I read it, it seemed to me that it is only he who could have told you that. What is the source of this information, that he decided to wait at least ten days?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he actually did wait until the 3rd of May. It was on the 3rd of May that he raised the issue of resubordination and the need to review it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, let's read this sentence, General. You say that the Chief of the General Staff decided to wait for at least ten days, especially as the president had read that also in the combat report of SVK that the Supreme Command received daily. In other words, you said he decided to wait ten days because of, especially because of something. How did you know that he decided to wait ten days for that reason unless he told you that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I know he had decided to speak to him only the 3rd of May, and that's 12 or 13 days from the order on resubordination. The order on subordination was issued on the 17th, and this happened on the 3rd. If he addressed the president on the 3rd, that means he had decided not to do it earlier. It is completely clear to me that it was his decision to wait for a while, expecting that the order would ultimately start working, that with the passage of time resubordination would take place as planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm focusing on the reason that you gave for the decision. You know the reason he made the decision? You haven't explained that, it seems to me, how you know the reason. Let's look at paragraph 214 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before you do that, you say in your answer: "I know he had decided to speak to him only on the 3rd of May ..." How did you know that? We know that he did. You may be able to say that he did speak to him on the 3rd of May and not before that, but how do you know he had decided to speak to him on the 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is a style and the style reflects the man, that's how I formulated it. Maybe it can be expressed in another way. That's the way I expressed it. If the person did not do that before the 3rd, that means to me that it was his decision to wait for things to settle down and maybe start working, but since they hadn't he decided to raise the issue on the 3rd. That's the way I worded it. It doesn't mean that it's the best possible way of putting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is from the top of my head, but is it not possible that he had been trying to see Milosevic and there was no suitable occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is possible, too, but I'm more inclined to think that he had decided to let a certain time pass because with that kind of order against the background of two different systems, it doesn't necessarily start working immediately. And after receiving information from various sides, he ultimately decided to bring that issue up again. That's the way I worded it, but it's not necessarily the best way. It can be put in a different way as well I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it convenient to break now or do you want to continue with the other question you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's convenient to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's convenient to break now, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we have to have a break now at this stage, Mr. Radinovic, as yesterday, so will you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One matter before the witness comes back in, Mr. Stamp, I heard you mention the constraints of time when you were asking questions of the witness. This is not a situation as we see it where because Mr. Visnjic uses 15 minutes and then a report which is the equivalent of a 92 ter statement, that you have an obligation to confine yourself if possible to a particular amount of time. I can make it clear now that I will have a number of questions for the witness on various areas. Now, with that guidance, can you give us some indication of timing so that appropriate arrangements can be made for the witness in case he has to stay a bit longer than anticipated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think in that case it's probable that he will have to return tomorrow because I would take up most, I think, of the day, if not all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I understand that was concerning you, Mr. Visnjic. It's a matter for you to make appropriate arrangements, but I think it highly likely that he will be here tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't believe that will be a problem. I just needed to know and to hear from Mr. Stamp where he might finish today so that we might organize something. Otherwise, there's no problem at all but of course as expeditiously as we can manage it would be the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We can have the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said at paragraph 19, page 66 of the report, and I'll just read the sentence. You made an assertion and then you said that: "That can be concluded on the basis of the fact that Ojdanic did not attend a single meeting with S. Milosevic at which a decision the future engagement of the army was taken." On what basis do you make this statement of fact that he never attended a meeting with Slobodan Milosevic where such matters were discussed? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis from the minutes of the meetings of the Supreme Defence Council, in which it is indicated who were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But the statement here does not indicate that you are speaking about meetings of the Supreme Defence Council. It speaks -- it says "a single meeting," meeting in general. Are you saying now that you're referring to meetings of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is only at those meetings that decisions about the use of the army can be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I take it your answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said that General Ojdanic did not attend meetings at which decisions are taken on the engagement of the army. Now, whether he had private meetings, I don't know, nor could I know, nor was I able to follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also said at paragraph 214, page 149, in respect to an aide-memoire that he ordered to be drafted -- to be drawn up: "Its production instilled fresh confidence both in those implementing it and the Chief of General Staff, chief of the Supreme Command Staff, who was permanently worried that violations of international law and humanitarian law might occur."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me where you're quoting from. I haven't managed to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's paragraph 214 at page 149, that's the second section.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 132 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, these are statements about --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not page 132. It is page 129.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Those are statements about his state of mind: Production instilled fresh confidence in him and that he was permanently worried, who told you about that? How did you know what he was thinking?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody told me. It was my conclusion drawn on the basis of demands made repeatedly for respect of ethic warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's turn to another area of your report. You speak, and to save time I won't go into each and every one. You speak I think from paragraphs -- paragraph 115 at page 41 in the English version forward about the motives and objectives of the NATO involvement and you make certain conclusions.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page are you referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm afraid I have the English page, paragraph 115 in the first section.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The conclusions and the facts that you assert in respect to the NATO involvement, I think you indicate on the basis of footnote 61 were arrived at from a magazine of the VJ, Novi Glasnik, and I think if you look at footnote 61 that's the --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These have been controversial matters here to some degree. Did you consider what General Naumann and Ambassador Petritsch said in respect to the involvement of NATO and the negotiations leading up to the involvement of NATO in March, did you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did take into consideration what they said. But I abided by the operative reports and to the General Staff, that was for me of greater relevance than Petritsch and Naumann.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, what you cited here in respect to that section were not the operative reports --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. [Interpretation] Page 39, the witness said operative reports and assessments of the General Staff, page 39, line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You don't, in your report, refer to any aspect of what General Naumann or Ambassador Petritsch had to say about the NATO intervention, do you? Well, I represent that you do not. The question is this: As an expert, where there are matters of controversy, would it not have been appropriate if you would decide to reject one side of the controversy, to analyse it in your report and explain why you decided to reject it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A serious handicap for my report which cannot be made up for is the fact that I didn't have the operative documents of NATO and the KLA. That is the most relevant part of the documents that was missing. Unfortunately, I couldn't make up for this because I didn't have these documents. Everything else is of lesser significance. If I had analysed the views of all those who had made comments about that conflict, I would never have completed the report. I simply chose this line of approach. My primary source are the operative documents and secondary documents only to the extent necessary when the primary documents were lacking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you know in this case that General Naumann and Ambassador Petritsch testified about these events that you submit in many pages of your report stating facts and conclusions upon. You're saying you think it is appropriate - and I'd like to read what you said - merely to adopt a line of approach of using the documents from the VJ, from one side of the controversy, to draw your conclusions. You think that is appropriate for an expert to do?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then you haven't heard a part of my answer. It is my conviction that this was necessary because I didn't have the documents of the other side, because only then if I had those documents would my report be fully credible. And only then could we discuss the issue. Unfortunately, I didn't receive those documents; why, I don't know, it isn't clear to me. I did ask the other side for those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you looked at what Naumann said. What -- what document in respect to General Naumann did you analyse or study?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now whether it was a report or a minute or transcript. I really can't remember. I don't even know exactly what he said, I can't remember now. If you have a specific source in mind, then you can ask me for my opinion about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm asking about methodology now. If we were to go into what --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained the methodology. You may agree with me or not. You may say this is not a good methodology, but it was my methodology. I felt that for a serious analysis I needed to have the sources of both sides, which I didn't. I only had the sources of one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, I make no judgement about your methodology, rest assured on that. I'm just asking questions right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the transcript, on page 41, line 3, the witness said I asked for these documents from the office, not from the other side, he probably meant the attorney's office and not from the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall what documents in respect to these negotiations that you spoke about in this part of your report emanating from Ambassador Petritsch that you analysed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could have seen in my report that I did not engage in negotiations, except to the extent they provided a general context for the command role of General Ojdanic. I didn't deal with Rambouillet either, I just noted it as an event that preceded the war in 1999 because I didn't feel that that was the subject of my expertise. Because this would have led me to analyse arguments that are outside this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but you are not focused on the question I asked. You make many statements about the background leading up to the international intervention in Kosovo. You met with the Defence and you know - this is what you have said - that Ambassador Petritsch had much to say about that. All I'm asking is this: What documents emanating from Ambassador Petritsch or representing what Ambassador Petritsch has said about these matters did you analyse?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not analyse the documents of Ambassador Petritsch.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told me earlier that you did I think. Anyway, be that as it may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Radinovic, were you asked to read any of the evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you asked to read any of the transcripts of evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't asked to. I did read some of the transcripts, I followed the proceedings on the internet, and I am relatively well-informed about what went on in these proceedings. But I had to make a selection of documents. I do refer to transcripts of some testimonies in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You made various unsubstantiated statements in the report, paragraphs 135, page 46; paragraph 116; paragraph 117; paragraph 134, we don't have time to go through all of them, but these are about NATO's motives in the bombardment, NATO's targeting in the bombardment, and I don't see where you have considered the press releases from NATO in respect to these bombardments. Did you consider these documents giving a different perspective that were available -- available to the public at the time? Or I should ask you: Weren't you aware that NATO gave press releases on a daily basis on the bombing of targets in Serbia? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the fact that the porte-parole made daily statements and I heard some of them, but that is not documentation that I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What's a porte-parole, I beg your pardon --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jamie Shea, porte-parole of NATO, spokesman, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take your answer that notwithstanding these many paragraphs in making statements in your report, your expert report about NATO and its motives and objectives, you were not interested in what they had to say, that is your answer, you were not interested in their contemporaneous representations of their motives. Can I ask you if I can move on, have you --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to answer this question with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the very last moment, that is, until I finished the first version of my report, I had expected to receive NATO reports. There's no reasonable reason for me not to receive them. I didn't study newspaper reports. I wanted the documents, the relevant documents, so I didn't ignore things. I was expecting to receive the real, the relevant documents. But to tell you the truth, I avoid using newspaper articles, only if I have absolutely no other source, then as an indication I may use them. But newspapers are, in principle, an unreliable source.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You're expecting to receive these relevant documents from whom?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Defence offices, the Defence counsel office. It was their duty to provide me with documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, let's not blame the Defence. Do you know that NATO has an official web site, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even lesser-important institutions have a web site. I'm quite sure NATO does.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But I'm a conservative sort of person, I'm quite advanced in age. I use a pencil. I don't use a PC. I'm simply that sort of person. You can crucify me, but that's who I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. So that is why I take it that you never consulted the official NATO web site, to get their version of events so that you could analyse them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did look and request their official documents on the basis of which they intervened so that we could see what went on, and if I -- as I didn't receive that, why would I look for newspapers and internet presentations which --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which in my view cannot be treated as a primary source.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is why I'm directing you now to focus on the official NATO web site that you said you're aware of. I just want you for the record to tell us whether or not you did not look at it to see what they were saying about their motivations. So it's either: Yes, you do; no, you did not. And I just want that for the record.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I felt, indeed, the results of what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that emotion which you just expressed has impacted on the manner in which you prepare your report, in the sense that you do not refer to what the NATO or what the international bodies have to say about those events that you described; is that correct, that you were affected -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no. I don't agree with you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- In your general assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said if I have the results of what NATO did, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the bombardment of the country. I personally, emotionally, in material terms, in every other respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In material terms, personally, and emotionally, surely that doesn't need any further elaboration. This is common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
