utterances.text: I understand that, but what I thought you're saying because you said it in response to a question I asked you about NATO sources of information is that you were saying based on the emotional, personal effects of the result of the NATO bombing you did not reflect upon NATO's version of the events. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you -- you spoke about the use of depleted uranium in your report. Now, I may or may not agree with you what you have to say, I'm not asking you about the truth of what you're saying in respect to the depleted uranium. What are your sources for your assertions in respect to that? You didn't give us that in your report.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the Novi Glasnik, there's a chapter in there dealing with depleted uranium --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you took your -- you took your facts from that magazine, which advocates a position of the Yugoslav Army, without citing it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by advocating or quoting. Let me explain what I have to say by your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question. What I'm saying -- what I'd like to ask you is this: Do you have any personal expertise in -- or study in depleted uranium?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, no, I'm not an expert on depleted uranium. I simply referred to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- In Novi Glasnik there's something about it. I think I also saw a document sent by NATO concerning places targeted by depleted uranium in Serbia with -- and these were the facts that I based my conclusion on. As you can see, I did not go into this in detail. I simply listed it as one of the consequences. I didn't delve into it any further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, with respect, you did not simply list it as one of your conclusions; you spent at least two paragraphs discussing it. Do you feel at liberty to insert into your report matters that fall outside of what you have just told us now, your field of expertise, do you feel at liberty to do so?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The consequences of the NATO aggression of course belong in this military expert report, but they are not the central topic. They simply provide the context for General Ojdanic's activity, and that's the extent to which I dealt with them. I simply listed the consequences indicating the sort of consequences they were, what their significance was, what they meant, referring of course to the experts who described them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on. You -- did you have any experience in the -- in a command position in the General Staff at any time in your career?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are no command positions in the General Staff, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But leading positions, yes. In 1984, or rather, 1983 to 1986 I was chief of a section in the operative administration of the General Staff, and the name of the section was the section for development and military doctrine. And that was a time when the then-Yugoslav Army was about to embark on a large-scale organization. I was in charge of that project in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Have you command experience of operational or strategic groups?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You spoke about Grom 98 or -- before I move on to that topic I think perhaps we should talk a little bit more about the responsibilities of General Ojdanic. You sought, it seemed to me, at paragraphs 176 to 177 - and that's in the second part, you sought to assert that General Ojdanic had no ability to exert his influence, his personal influence, on units in the field. If you look at the last couple sentences in paragraph 176 you will see that that is exactly what you said. However, is it not true that he could nonetheless as Chief of General Staff exert his influence on the activities in the field, particularly in Kosovo, notwithstanding that he was 3 or 400 miles away, through various instruments like inspections and a proper reporting chain, could he not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I said. I said that was the only he could exert an influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As -- he could call on the commanders in the field to report to him, could he not, if he so desired?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He could send appropriate senior personnel to the field to make investigations and inspections, could he not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he could talk to the commanders in the field by radio, by a wire, and by other means, could he not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he could, but I don't know whether he did or not. He could, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He could suspend commanders in the field, could he not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he had reason to do so, he could. I never found any reason for him to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So maybe I just had the wrong impression. You will agree with me, therefore, that although he, because of some circumstances you describe, found it impractical to himself going to the field, based on the established rules he still had effective control of his commanders in the field?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether he had effective control or not, I don't know. That's for someone else to establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, no --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- What I tried to show here is what kind of control he could have had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you -- you are the expert, you reviewed the documents, you --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You should be --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I reviewed all the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- You should be able to answer that question whether it is your view that he had effective control of his commanders in the field or whether he was a general who did not have effective command of his commanders in the field?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusion, which I stated in the report is that within the scope of his competence he carried out his job very well and he carried out all his duties very efficiently, all within the sphere of his competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it then --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Using the methods and means he had at his disposal, that is, reports, controls, or inspections, and preventive action.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He was the Chief of General Staff who was in charge of and responsible for the preparation of plans Grom 2 and 3 -- well, plans Grom or code-named Grom in January and February 1999, was he not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grom 3 in January, I'm sure that Grom 1998 had two stages: Grom 1 and Grom 2. Grom 3 was only from January 1999, and it refers to the prevention of forcible entry of a multi-national brigade into Kosovo. Grom 1 was protecting the state border and Grom 2 was breaking up the terrorist Siptar forces should there be a mass armed rebellion. One can say then that General Ojdanic -- well, that Grom 3 was developed under his mandate, whereas Grom 1 and Grom 2 were developed previously under Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Are you aware that before the NATO intervention on the 24th of March he deployed units into Kosovo for activities against the KLA, and that's in February and early March 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of this, but I would have to see what document this is about and then we can discuss it. I know that this did happen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you know that he deployed troops from outside of Kosovo into Kosovo for engagements against the KLA in February and March 1999 prior to the NATO intervention?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that, and as far as I was able to follow this process -- these proceedings, General Krga testified about this in greater detail and I have nothing to add to what he said. I anticipated what he said in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We'll return to that. I wish to take you to paragraph 58 and the succeeding paragraphs. That's paragraph 58 at page 87, so I think it would be the second part of part -- this is under the chapter: "The chain of command in the 1999 war." And I think your thesis is that the General Staff was not a level of command in the VJ. I think that's what you said in paragraph 57.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said another paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And further at paragraph 64 you say that the Chief of General Staff had no effective command competence over strategic formations.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me what part this refers to so I can see exactly what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that in paragraph 64?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's 64 to 66 I see here, I'm sorry, I probably should just read the passage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In paragraph 64 you said: "Pursuant to this article," and that's article 6 which we will come to, "the unequivocal conclusion follows that the chief of General Staff does not have direct competence of command that it automatically flow from his position in the chain of command as is the case with commands and commanders at all levels but the Chief of General Staff has his control competencies which are below the command level. Everything pertaining to the Chief of General Staff powers in respect of command and this primarily refers to the issues of certain command documents is linked to the powers of the president of the republic." Then at paragraph 66 you go on to say: "Thus a chain that is a vertical chain of command in the VJ went from the VSO as the Supreme Command and the president of the FRY the supreme commander, the commands of the armies, the air force and the air defence, and navy commands as the commands of the strategic groups and from them to the corps commanders." So you are saying that the Chief of General Staff had no command competencies over these strategic formations, is that correct, in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So he --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. You're reading one thing and concluding something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us then, what are his command competencies from -- that you're referring to that he has?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The General Staff under the Law on the Army in Article 5 is a professional staff organ for the preparation and the use of the army. That's the definition of the General Staff, and based on this I drew conclusions on the command authorities in this case of General Ojdanic, and I said that this article defining the General Staff cannot be interpreted in such a way as to establish that the General Staff is a separate level of command. Rather, it is an expert or professional and staff element of command. In the professional or expert sense, it deals with preparation, deployment, equipping, and building up the army. In the staff part of its activities, it deals with planning, operative planning, plans of use, proposing decisions, and so on. That's the sphere of activity of the General Staff. It is not a command, it is not a command. Had the legislator envisaged it as a command, the legislator would have defined it as such. So I can only say what it says in the legislation and also in doctrinal terms. This is how it is in all armies everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Maybe --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me digress a little. There's a wonderful book called: "The brain of the army" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know whether this will cause problems later on because of the interpretation, but on page 53, line 5, the General said "rukovodna ovlastenja." I think it's different -- this refers to control, not command. So these are two different terms and two different concepts. To avoid confusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the position is noted. The witness has heard what you've said, but it is a matter you can also raise in re-examination if it's controversial as it may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just worried about translation and maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, it's one I think to be clarified later if you feel it's still necessary. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You are speaking about the staff, General Staff. The question I asked you was about the command competencies of General Ojdanic, the Chief of General Staff. So -- and the question was: What are his command competencies in respect to the strategic groups, the armies, for example, the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of General Staff, that is, the chief of Supreme Command Staff in wartime, has towards the 3rd Army command exactly the role prescribed for him as the Chief of the General Staff; that is, he receives information from the 3rd Army command as to what they're doing he receives information from combat reports, inspection reports, et cetera, and on that basis he studies the enemy and prepares proposals for the supreme commander as to how to engage the 3rd Army. Once the supreme commander accepts these proposals, the Chief of General Staff or the chief of Supreme Command Staff is then duty-bound to implement this in the form of appropriate directives, orders, commands, et cetera, addressed to the 3rd Army and the 3rd Army is duty-bound to execute them. In that sense, the Chief of General Staff has great control powers, but here I dealt with the distinction between control and command, and I refuted the assertion that the General Staff was a separate level of command, it is not. It is instead a professional and staff organ within the Supreme Command with great control powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I understand --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a professional issue, it's not easy to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a professional matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you're saying that the Chief of the General Staff does not have direct command competencies then in respect to the armies?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He has them only as the chief of Supreme Command Staff, and only in the measure in which he is authorised to have them as [as interpreted] the supreme commander, that is, the president of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Maybe we could clarify this with a look at the documents. Well, firstly, Article 6 of the Law of Defence which you quote in paragraph 62 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, just for the clarification, 55, 16, I believe instead of to have them as the supreme commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: By --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It should say by the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Article 6 which you quote in paragraph 62 --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we see that Article 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You quote it in paragraph 62 of your report.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the Law on the Army, not the Law on Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It says: "For the execution of documents brought in by the president of the republic and of duties of commanding the army as well as duties laid down under this law, the Chief of General Staff shall bring in rules, orders, commands, instructions, and similar documents." I ask you is this saying that the Chief of General Staff shall bring rules, orders, and commands for the execution of his duties in commanding the army? Doesn't Article 6 say he has command and commands the army?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It does not --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Article 6 does not say that say that he has command over the army. It's rather that the three key documents: The constitution, the Law on the Army, and the Law on Defence say instead, stipulate instead, that it is the head of state that commands the army in keeping with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. The General Staff is not mentioned at all. Speaking of original competence for command, the General Staff is not in the picture. The General Staff is in the picture as the professional and staff organ of the army without which the army cannot function, nor can it play its role. And indeed, the General Staff has great powers and responsibility. Like all General Staffs of the world, it has that great professional and staff role.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I agree with you, General, that the commander, the supreme commander, is the president of the republic. What I take issue, just to be clear, is that I think you make the assertion in the report that the Chief of the General Staff has no direct command competencies as Chief of the General Staff in respect to the armies and other strategic groups. I'd like to -- you to have a look at a particular document and comment on it, it's P1041. Perhaps we could start with the -- just have a look at the first page there in B/C/S and read it for us. May I just say the first page in B/C/S does not appear on e-court in English. Could you just read --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. You mean the curriculum and syllabus?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you read what is on the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Curriculum and syllabus for post-graduate studies leading to the academic degree of bachelor of science at the military academy of the Army of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could we go to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Tactics" was the last word on the front page. Can you zoom in a bit so I can see better?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we go to page 7 in the B/C/S. This is in the English version for some reason.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is some kind of certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A candidate, a reader, at post-graduate studies --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just indicate that the document is a manual of command and control in the VJ, but the -- there are some parts of it in e-court which are not accurate. That needs to be rectified. I only discovered this last night, but -- and some parts of it are not in the English version. But there we have page 7. Can you tell us what that -- who the authors are of this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These names don't mean anything to me. I don't know when this was done. It must have been at a time when I was no longer in the army. I know some of these people. I happen to know the expert editor, Professor Milan Karajovic. I know Mrs. Radonjic, who was the linguistic editor. I don't know the others, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who is the expert editor Professor Major-General Karajovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while he was chief of personnel, later chief of the military academy; unfortunately, he died about a year ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we have a look at page 97 in the English e-court which corresponds to page 138 in the B/C/S e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you look at paragraph 2.3.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They retell Article 5 of the Law on the Army. The first sentence is practically copied from that article.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just have a look at it. There's one part of it. The last two sentences of this section read -- reads -- read that -- and we have take all of this in context, but I just want to focus on the last two sentences. "The commanders of armies, the air force, and anti-aircraft defence, and the navy are responsible to the Chief of General Staff of the army, as are the commandants of units and temporary compositions immediately subordinate to him," I stress the words "immediately subordinate to him in the execution of the affairs of command and control," and I stress the word "command and control of the army put into a sphere of competence by law and other regulations and in the accomplishment of instruments of command of the president of FRY, the Chief of the General Staff of the army commands the army via commandants of the strategic units and temporary strategic compositions and other officers who are immediately subordinate to him." Do you agree with that statement as to the competencies of the Chief of General Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On certain points I don't agree with this because it interprets the place of General Staff in the system of commanding the army beyond what I analysed and evaluated, and I believe beyond the Article 5 of the Law on the Army. Another thing, this is a manual and a manual is a temporary document for decision-making and for training and education, and what is relevant to me is interpretation of the laws and principles of doctrine. This as a manual is a lower-ranking document and I see the role of the General Staff a bit differently to what is described here and I have already tried to explain that in answering the previous question of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have you reviewed the manual of command and control of the VJ before?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you review this part of it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you're saying that your opinion is higher-ranking to the manual of the VJ, manual of command and control of the VJ; that is your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not what I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only said that the sources I invoked and referred to -- well, don't put words in my mouth that I didn't say. I have to respond when you are trying to misrepresent my evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, I am not. I just want to know if you thought that the -- your opinion was at a higher ranking level. That's the expression you used. You said it was a lower-ranking document. That's why I asked, and I am only asking questions, if you thought your opinion --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is of lower relevance than the law and the rules of procedure. The original authentic document's ruling military organization and its functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is the manual circulated to members of the command of the various commands of the various strategic and operational formation of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know because I was not in the army at the time when this was written, but I don't think it is compulsory. I think it is kept in libraries that exist attached to every command. It is available material. I don't think this was distributed, but I'm just speculating.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyway, there is no need to distribute it on a compulsory basis to commanding officers when it is available in the library. It is not a document that they should be guided by.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But do they study that command staff training programmes? Is it a part of the curriculum of study for command staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I trained them, and I used to head the department of strategy in the school of national defence, I taught them about the General Staff as an expert in staff organ, not the way they are teaching here. You have heard from other very competent witnesses opinions that differ from mine, but this is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I represent to you that this manual is dated 1997 and was the -- was operative at the relevant time. When did you teach?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I taught before 1993, unfortunately or luckily I was retired in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You taught in the days of the old JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and in the Army of Yugoslavia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You will agree with me that the period of the 1990s in the JNA and Army of Yugoslavia was a period of ferment, if you can call it that, things were boiling up and changing at a very rapid pace after you retired; you will agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all the changes that happened before I retired remained in place afterwards all the way until 1999. Nothing changed in that period. I left the Army of Yugoslavia. I was retired from the Army of Yugoslavia where the General Staff was headed by General Ojdanic. Nothing changed there in the organization and the establishment, although the people changed. During my service, the Law on Defence, the Law on the Army, the constitution were already adopted, all that happened while I was still in the army and I was in the position of head of department for strategy in the department -- in the Ministry of Defence, so I followed these things.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Strategy and policy, Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have had evidence from a variety of people in this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 62, line 3, I think the General said that he was retired from the same army in which General Ojdanic served, not the army commanded by General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the same army I said in which General Ojdanic was Chief of General Staff in 1999. Nothing had changed from my retirement until 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General Ojdanic has signed a significant amount of orders that we have. He does not sign them as a delegate of the supreme commander, of the president, he signs them in his own capacity as chief of the Supreme Command, Chief of the General Staff. Does that indicate to you that he had independent command and was not like a Chief of Staff of a strategic or operational group?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try to simplify things. If the Supreme Defence Council and the president of the state had supreme command, then what kind of supreme command would be in the hands of Chief of General Staff if he were commanding military formations? That would be a classical case of parallel tracks. That's why the General Staff had the role of an expert and staff body with great responsibility and great competences. But their command competences were only delegated to them by the president of the republic. Any enactments of command were issued by the General Staff only on the authority of the president of the supreme commander. That's what I know. I know of course that General Ojdanic issued and signed all kinds of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We know that the president of the FRY was the supreme commander and General Ojdanic would have to act within the ambit of the authority of the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the law. But do you know of any law or regulation that describes General Ojdanic's role as a delegate of the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What exists is the Law on the Army from which you can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, when you say you can see that, that is your interpretation or the interpretation that you represent to us now?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only give you my interpretation; I can't give you anybody else's. That's my reading of the law and legislative enactments governing command, and you invited me here as an expert. I cannot speak in any other role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We had some discussion yesterday about the execution of tasks given to officers at lower level, and it was plain from your evidence and indeed other evidence in this case that the officer who has a task to undertake has a discretion in how to do, and he has authority over the various units which are further down the scale than he is. Is it conceivable that the supreme commander or the Supreme Defence Council might decide, issue a decision, to the effect that the KLA have to be attacked with all forces available to the Yugoslav Army and give that instruction to the Chief of the General Staff to execute and leave it to him to decide what instructions to give to the various armies to carry out that task? Or is that just an inconceivable hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Supreme Command issues and makes strategic decisions, whereas the Supreme Command Staff proposes decisions. Thus, the Supreme Command does not have an apparatus that would actually draft decisions or documents; that's what the Supreme Command Staff does. And that is where the chief comes in. He prepares the decision on deployment and engagement of the army. He submits that draft for approval to the president, that is, the supreme commander. And once the president agrees and approves, then the Chief of the General Staff and the chief of the Supreme Command Staff start elaborating it together with their staff and conveying it to the subordinates. That's the mechanism of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's one thing just to look at the 3rd Army in isolation, but the example I'm giving you envisages the use of all forces, so you've got the 1st, the 2nd, the 3rd Army, you have the navy and the air force. Once this decision is made and issued, who actually coordinates the activities of these various groups? There must be some overall commander who is then executing the supreme commander's order. Now, how does that -- how would that work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the job of the Supreme Command Staff, the operative coordination is performed by the Supreme Command Staff, and that's where the chief of the Supreme Command Staff has a key role. But all my interventions, all my writing regarding the Chief of General Staff or the chief of Supreme Command Staff were geared to indicate that it was not a parallel command. They cannot have direct command over the armies if it is the supreme commander who has direct command of the armies. That cannot be true. That was why I said that what is written in the manual cannot be quite true. You defined it very well. It is precisely that role that the Supreme Command Staff has. After a decision a made, the Supreme Command Staff has the job of coordinating everything at the level of strategic groups and prepares decisions for follow-up actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now we may be going to part company. That sounds to me like giving the Chief of the General Staff command competencies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He does have competencies. He's not without any kind of responsibility in that sense, but that responsibility has been delegated to him. It is not original to his post. It has been delegated to him by the Supreme Command. Of course he has responsibilities in that sense. As for -- he is responsible for the behaviour of the commanders of strategic groups, certainly, there's no dispute about that. I'm just saying that the General Staff is not a separate command level, because if it was a separate level then it would have to be above the whole army, then above whom would the Supreme Command be and the supreme commander? So his professional staff is the professional body. When we're talking about the use of the army, the General Staff takes over all the operative functions, planning, organizational, control, and everything else that relates to collective [as interpreted] decision-making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand entirely your point about parallel lines of command, but is what you're describing now not simply or does it not simply put the Chief of the General Staff into the chain of command but under the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's certainly in the Supreme Command. He cannot dissociate himself from what is happening in the system of strategic command. I never claimed anything like that. It is quite clear to me. I'm endeavouring to convey this position of mine. The General Staff in peacetime practically has control over everything happening in the army because the supreme commander deals with statesmanship, he doesn't deal with the army. But when we're talking about command we have in mind primarily wartime or other extraordinary situations, emergencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You didn't really, I don't think, address my question. I'm asking you whether it's not appropriate to simply regard the Chief of the General Staff, and indeed the General Staff, as part of the chain of command that comes in somewhere between the supreme commander and the various army groupings, 1st, 2nd, 3rd, air force, and navy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that is not my understanding, and I'm trying to explain why I differ. It is a component part of the Supreme Command. It is its working body, its operational staff. Like any other command at any level, at the brigade level, the army, it has its staff, and this staff works for the needs of the command at that level. So it is a component part of the Supreme Command, and if we were to show it in diagram form, it would be in the same box, both the Supreme Defence Council, the president, and the Supreme Command, it is all one level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before Mr. Stamp continues, a small correction, page 66, line 12, I don't wish to interrupt, it says "collective," and it should be "corrective."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my colleague tells me now 67, line 15 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 15 of page 67, the Supreme Defence Council, the president, the Supreme Command, and the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. It would be convenient to break, Mr. Stamp, but if you have something following on from that you can deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It would probably take five minutes so I think it would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we'll just break then?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need to break again, Mr. Radinovic, and this will be for half an hour and we'll see you again at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to try to move very quickly, so I'm going to ask you to try to limit your answers to just as precise a response as necessary. We have had evidence before the Court that in the course of the conflict with NATO, General Ojdanic had daily briefings with the staff and they considered reports that had been sent up from the strategic formations, armies, et cetera, and he immediately issued orders for the staff to draw up and send down to these strategic units. Now, if he had the power to issue these orders and did so, yet you're saying that the supreme commander was a person to whom these strategic units, the strategic formations, were directly responsible to or directly below, would that not indicate a parallel chain of command contrary to the principle which you referred to, the principle of singleness of command?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not. Then you haven't understood me well. I have done my best to explain here that the General Staff is a working body or the staff of the Supreme Command, and that on that basis it does what it does. There's no parallelism. If the General Staff was what you say it was, then there would be a parallel command, parallel chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I suggest to you that the General Staff, the Chief of the General Staff was in the chain of command acting pursuant to the orders of the supreme commander but was responsible to command the armies and the strategic groups, as is indicated in the manual of command and control for the VJ. I do not say that there was a parallel command; I am saying that there was a chain of command. And what I'm saying is consistent with the manual of command and control. What I ask you is that if he as Chief of General Staff could issue orders independently to these strategic formations, and according to you the supreme commander, the president, could also do the same, then it is your proposition which would lead to a parallel command?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is your opinion but I don't share it. There is no way I can dissuade you, I'm trying to but obviously I'm not successful, and I'm helpless. But I wish to say the following: You, yourself said on a daily basis, every morning, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command with prepared combat reports for the whole army and with proposals of decisions went to the supreme commander. And in direct contact with him, he would be given authorisation to act. Of course he was in the chain of command. There's no dispute about it, but not as a separate level, rather, as a component part of the strategic level of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think that's how Mr. Stamp worded his question. You may have misunderstood the question, and he was referring to the evidence in the case of daily briefings among the generals or others with responsibility at the Supreme Command Staff where they considered reports sent up from strategic formations. And immediately there on the spot orders were issued by General Ojdanic. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If that's the evidence in the case, how do you explain it consistently with your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether you heard evidence and heard testimony that every morning the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command went to see the supreme commander, presenting the conclusions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have not had that evidence, it is conspicuous by its absence. It is your understanding that every day General Ojdanic met Mr. Milosevic in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every day in the morning General Ojdanic reported on combat reports of the Supreme Command Staff regarding the situation in the whole army to the supreme commander every morning; that was the practice. And those minutes exist, I've seen them. I don't know why you don't have that in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where did you get minutes of daily meetings with General Ojdanic and President Milosevic? Where did you get those minutes from?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not daily meetings with President Milosevic, but daily briefings of the chief of the supreme staff, on the basis of which a report was compiled for the Supreme Command and that report was reported to the supreme commander. That was the method of work of the Supreme Command during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, are you aware of the documents to which the witness is referring so that we can clear this up? It may be I'm missing something.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my understanding, the witness - let me clear up what I know, that minutes from the briefings between Milosevic and Ojdanic do not exist, I know that for certain. But my understanding is he's talking about the evening meetings on the basis of which the morning briefings took place, and those minutes have been provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The evening meetings with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Evening briefings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness is talking about briefings given to the supreme commander, that is, to Milosevic. Now, do you know what documents he is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which documents he's referring to and I don't know that those documents -- I do know those documents don't exist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about combat reports of the army which the general -- which the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command reported to the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, at the moment I do not know what you're talking about. I do not think we have seen such document -- well, Mr. O'Sullivan is going to prove me wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There's just one comment I would like to make in response to something you said at line 18 on page 70 and your comment was: "We have not had that evidence in response to morning briefings between the chief of the staff and the supreme commander." My recollection is we do have evidence of morning meetings between General Ojdanic and President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan, that's something that's not clear in my mind at the moment, but I will refresh myself by reference to the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think, sir, what caused the problem was not morning meetings with President Milosevic, but what you said every day in the morning General Ojdanic reported on combat reports to the supreme commander regarding the situation of the whole army to the supreme commander every morning, you repeated that, so the clarification exists. "That was the practice. And those minutes exist, I've seen them. I don't know why you don't have that in evidence." That --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was thinking of combat reports of the Supreme Command Staff which summarize the situation in the army and which are submitted to the supreme commander, and the supreme commander puts questions about it and the other one answers those questions. That is the normal process of briefing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the way Mr. Stamp put his question I'm also confused. He said that President Milosevic -- that, rather, General Ojdanic informs President Milosevic every day about combat reports, and he said that was the practice and such minutes exist and that he saw those minutes. Now, I don't know whether Mr. Stamp has seen those minutes on meetings between President Milosevic and General Ojdanic or is he talking about the combat reports of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All Mr. Stamp was doing was quoting the witness's answer as translated into English, and the witness said these words which are there in the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, then it's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I think the witness understands that. But before we go on any further, can I ask you, Mr. O'Sullivan, just to remind me where this evidence is of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My recollection is it's one of the Ojdanic witness's testified to that effect. Right now I can't give you the name, it may have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to find the name, Your Honour, General Curcin, he was the last one, but there were several before him, all of them from the operative administration have testified to that effect in a sense but I will give you a more precise name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that testimony that there were daily meetings between General Ojdanic and Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I apologise for my failure to take note of that as I ought to have done. Thank you for clarifying that. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I want to move pretty quickly. So what the record says is not correct. You have not seen minutes of daily meetings between General Ojdanic and Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that was not what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was what I said, I apologise, it was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Back to what I was asking you. The evidence is that there were briefings in the staff, the Supreme Command Staff, in which they received reports from the strategic units, discussed these reports, and General Ojdanic immediately gave what one witness described as very precise orders that were formulated or prepared by the staff and sent down back to these strategic formations. If, as you say, it was the president of the republic of the Federation, Mr. Milosevic, as supreme commander who had direct command powers over these strategic formations, wouldn't it mean that when General Ojdanic issued those orders independently and immediately, he would be acting parallel to the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he's acting in accordance with the competencies he has and in accordance with his position in the chain of strategic command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think -- I've just been informed that I made a point to refer that Mr. Visnjic is indeed correct that Mr. Curcin said there were daily meetings and that is at 16979 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said in support of your argument at paragraph 71, page 93, that the supreme commander received daily combat reports from the strategic groups?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me find it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: First two sentences of that paragraph. Where or what is your source of this information, that the supreme commander received daily combat reports from the strategic groups?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A combat report was compiled every day of the Supreme Command Staff summarizing the situation in all strategic groupings and in attachment the combat report of the 3rd Army, and there were other attachments as well, of course. With some reports of the Supreme Command Staff, there was also in attachment the report of the Pristina Corps so that the supreme commander could have the best possible insight into the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So where did he get -- what's the source of the information that he received the command -- he received the combat reports, what's the source of that information?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the last page of the combat report of the Supreme Command Staff, you see a list of the addressees. When the Supreme Command Staff prepares a combat report, then it is sent to the office of the Supreme Command Staff which then sends it on to the military committee of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So on the last page it is clearly indicated to whom those reports go, and you can see for yourself that he did receive those reports on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you if he received combat reports from the General Staff. I was asking you if he received those that were sent up to the staff by the strategic groups. Because the evidence we have had from General Ivkovic in 3D117, I say this for the record. And I think even in your report at 112, paragraph 12, is that the supreme commander, Mr. Milosevic, only got the summary report or the consolidated report prepared by the operations staff or the operations sector of the General Staff. Do you take issue with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't because in the combat report of the Supreme Command Staff, the most important things had to be contained, not everything, otherwise the report would consist of 25, 30 pages and that would be unnecessary. Of course it contains only the most important points, but attached to that report there are attachments by the command of the 3rd Army and sometimes also of the command of the Pristina Corps about the rear, the logistics, the replenishments, the NATO operations, everything -- all those things were attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on quickly if I could take you to paragraph 34 of your report, that's in page 72, so that's in part 2. The VSO, I take, it here refers to the Supreme Defence Council; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have page 72 here, as you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph 34 in part 2.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I apologise then. 34, page 66?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 66 in your copy. Referring to the second section -- second sentence: "Although the Supreme Defence Council sessions were almost regularly and since the beginning of the aggression were mandatorily attended by the federal minister of defence, the Chief of Staff of the VJ and very often the federal prime minister and others, none of them had either the status competence of a VSO member nor could in that sense participate in the VSO decision-making." The first thing I'd like to ask you about that is you said: "Since the beginning of the aggression they were mandatorily attended by the federal minister of defence ..." Were there meetings since the beginning of the aggression, of what you call the aggression? What do you mean when you say that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean is that according to the rules of procedure it was the duty of the VSO to have the minister and the Chief of General Staff attend. I never found any records during the aggression that a meeting of the VSO was held, if that was your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 66, part 2, and this is page 90 of the English version. You're saying here as an expert in paragraph 66: "Thus the chain of command, that is, the vertical of command in the VJ went from the VSO as the Supreme Command and the president of the FRY as the supreme commander to the commands of the armies ..." What do you mean when you say "went from the VSO as the Supreme Command ..."?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely what I said. In my view, the VSO was the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that's -- in other words, the composition of the Supreme Command was the same as the composition of the VSO?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was no other Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did I rightly understand you to say that they never met during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether they met or not, but I never found any documents that would convince me that they did meet. I assume such documents would be available were there any in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how do you see the decisions necessary for the conduct of the war having been taken in the absence of meetings of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Supreme Defence Council met in October, it met later as well, but the conclusions reached at the October session refer to the situation in the country in case of attack. It would defend itself by all means. Based on that decision, once a state of war was declared plans for the use of the army, or rather, the war plans could be activated. These plans had been drawn up in time. That conclusion was a mandate for starting to implement the plans of use in case the country's attacked. In view of that fact, there was no operative need, although I do admit it seems quite unnatural that the VSO did not meet on that occasion. I think it would have been natural for it to meet, but it did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the Supreme Defence Council have no say in determining the existence of a state of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A state of war is declared by the Assembly or by the federal cabinet if the Assembly is unable to meet. The VSO has the right of initiative but not the right to decide on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but is it the right to initiate it or the responsibility to initiate the determination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time, I really don't know whether the VSO initiated this or not, so I cannot answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does any other body have the right to initiate the determination of a state of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, under the constitution the federal cabinet initiates that decision and it's adopted by the Assembly. If the Assembly's unable to meet, then the federal cabinet declares a state of war on its own and the first time the Assembly is able to meet it verifies the decision. That's as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The war eventually came to an end. Did the Supreme Defence Council have no say in whether it should be brought to end or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether it met for that reason, I don't know, but the president of the state and of the VSO when President Milutinovic as a member of the VSO were very active in all the peace initiatives and in bringing the war to an end through the Kumanovo negotiations and agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And at paragraph 136, part 2, page 112 in English, do you see that the combat reports prepared by the Supreme Command Staff were distributed to persons including the president of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You spoke -- well, you wrote in your report - and I'm moving on to a different topic, if I may quickly - about steps taken by General Ojdanic to prevent and punish possible infractions of humanitarian law. And if I may refer you to paragraph 185 of your report you gave the reasons why General Ojdanic did so. This is 134 of the English version: "The reasons being they wanted to be absolutely sure that men and officers were familiar with the subject of international law of war; 2, the quantity and levels of crimes of the forces of the Albanian separatist movement of NATO strikes from a safe distance were such that the latest danger existed of crimes of vengeance ... 3, there were extensive negative experience from past wars on the soil of the former Yugoslavia and numerous war crimes on all warring sides ..." Surely you would think that there would be one other reason, that there was notice that the international community were saying and had said that armed forces of Serbia used excessive force in 1998 and the period leading up to the war that caused significant casualties to civilians and damage to civilian property. You know of those claims?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what I should be aware of here. Of course I know that there was a conflict, that in the course of the conflict there was destruction; those are unfortunately the consequences of every war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid we have an incomplete interpretation of my learned friend's question into B/C/S. It was not interpreted that there was use of excessive force, so could the question be either repeated or clarified. It was interpreted differently into B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see, the question is that surely any conscientious general would want to take steps to prevent and punish crimes against civilians because there had been reports and allegations by international organizations that the Serbian armed forces in 1998 and in a period going up to the war used excessive force against civilians?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I think I know this very well, nowhere in military doctrine or in the normative regulations is it prescribed to what extent force is not excessive; and when it's excessive, that's arbitrary. It depends --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- On a case-by-case assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are only certain kinds of weapons, certain numbers of shells that can be fired to achieve a certain goal of neutralising the other side. But there is nothing to say what is excessive and what is not excessive use of force. It's a matter of analysis in each individual case for that to be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I'm asking you, General Ojdanic would have been aware of, for example, United Nations Security Council Resolution 1199, which stated that there were 230-odd thousand IDPs in Kosovo as a result of indiscriminate and excessive use of force by Serbian forces, he would have been aware of this resolution, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, he knew that of course. But the question is there would have been the same number of displaced persons even had there been far less use of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because people flee from combat areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, you are an expert, so I know -- or I don't think you want to appear to be advocating some cause. Just, please, focus on what I'm asking you. The point is that the reasons, at least three of the reasons why it was important for a conscientious general to put in place provisions to prevent and punish crimes against the civilians existed before the NATO assault began on the 24th of March. And to move quickly, that is a statement and I'll ask a question on the basis of that statement --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I anticipated that in paragraph 3 or item 3. There were negative experiences from previous wars on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and of course that includes 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. When we look at your charts from page 144 to 148 in the English version, and that is at paragraph 210, part 2, of your version, on steps that General Ojdanic took, we see that in all of these charts these steps occurred during the war and almost all of them occurred after the incidents charged in this indictment occurred. You look at all of these charts. Having regard to the fact that you have in your report told us about General Ojdanic's conscientious building up of the forces in defence of the country, do you know of any reason why General Ojdanic failed or was unable to take these steps at the same time, that is, a period prior to the -- when the hostilities began when he would have been aware of the reasons why these steps were necessary? Why didn't he do them then? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he took a number of measures which were supposed to prevent possible crimes in Kosovo and Metohija. The whole system --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, they are not in your charts.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Why didn't you put the measures that he took before the war began in your charts?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a part that refers to training in humanitarian law, then there's the part on the normative activity. There's -- the chart was meant to illustrate the care General Ojdanic took and his concern for the behaviour of the army in Kosovo and Metohija. A number of orders were issued to prevent crimes, to warn commands and units. And as you know, before that a number of brochures and instructions were issued as to how they should behave on the territory in case of conflict with terrorist forces, how fighters should behave on the battle-field, how commanders should behave. And this is a whole series of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, this is a whole series of documents. The question is: Where are the specific orders made which predate the crimes charged in the indictment or which predate the commencement of hostilities? Your charts don't include them.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that there's a whole chapter dealing with education and training in international humanitarian law and the laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm trying to move quickly.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what sort of orders you are referring to. I really don't understand what you mean and what you expect me to reply to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Take a look at any one of those orders. These are the orders I'm referring to, those in your chart. Is there -- and this is the question: Is there any reason why any one of these specific orders could not have been made at a time when it was known, according to your report, that there would have been an assault by NATO? Is there any reason why they could not have been made? That is the question.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could have been issued then, but the Supreme Command Staff assessed that that was the right time to address the lower commands directly and to pre-empt any possible crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the part I paid attention to because I felt it was the most important part. It doesn't mean that there was nothing before and that no action was taken in that respect beforehand, but this is the material I felt I ought to include.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's discuss briefly what is described as an armed non-Siptar population, which you refer to at various parts of your report. Do you know approximately how many persons of Serb ethnicity were armed by the VJ in 1998 and the months prior to the beginning of the hostilities?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly at what collegium meeting I saw information about 47.000 armed civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I represent to you that that is what General Samardzic reported to General Ojdanic, so we won't need to take out that document. So when you speak in your report at paragraphs 73 to 74 and 76 as well of part 1 of your report, and this is at page 25 to 26 of the English, about the strength of the civilian protection and the civilian defence, I think in paragraph 73 you said for civilian protection 3.365; for civilian defence, 1.165 plus 423 plus 1.179, somewhere in the region of 3.000 again. What you are describing as civilian defence and civilian protection are distinction and different groupings from armed Serb civilians. You will agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, but it was as part of those 47.000. I agree they were different, but they were all part of that 47.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So when you at some point other in that section of the report indicate that civilian protection and civilian defence could not be used for combat tasks, there is another 40.000 armed Serbs that are not included in that group?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would like to explain something, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This group of 47.000 armed civilians that General Samardzic mentioned at the collegium should be seen as including all the members of the reserve -- army reservists, the military territorial units, the reserve MUP forces, to whom weapons were issued. And that 47.000 also includes units of civilian protection and civil defence and what is colloquially referred to as the armed non-Siptar population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are documents referring to that which I cited here. So all of that is included in that number. According to the demographic potential of Kosovo, it would be absolutely impossible to have 47.000 civilians who are completely outside the units of the army, police, civilian protection, civil defence. There weren't that many men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that was my calculation through which one can arrive at the information that you can't have 47.000 armed civilians who are not reservists of the army, the police, the civilian defence, civil protection, cryptographic protection, intelligence services, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You are repeating yourself. The component that you referred to as the -- or you say they were colloquially referred to as an armed non-Siptar population, how many of those were there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no data. Nobody ever did that calculation, but according to my own calculation which I have not presented in my report because I have no references on which I can base it with certainty, I have no corroboration for my calculation, but according to my own calculation, outside these four systems, army, police, civilian -- civil defence, and civilian protection, there could be between 5 and 6.000, not more. Because there wouldn't be enough men for a larger number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, we're already past the deadline. Is this a suitable time to interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It will be necessary, Mr. Radinovic, for you to return tomorrow. We will be sitting again at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Overnight please remember what I've said to you about non-communication on matters relating to the evidence. Now could you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 19th day of October, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
